title: Education Halfway Through a Pedagogy Degree Norma Sancho
author: Sancho, Norma
summary: A pedagogy student reflects midway through her degree on what educational theory has actually taught her — framed not as a recitation of the syllabus but as a reckoning with what each theorist reveals and where they fall short. Montessori's liberating pedagogy can become 'a small church if it stops listening.' Vygotsky insists education is always relational: you cannot design for adults in crisis as if they were solitary minds downloading content. Piaget's developmental stages became a fixed floor plan while technology kept remodeling the floor underneath — a four-year-old swiping a tablet before she can hold a pencil breaks the theory. Dewey makes experience serious: not every suffering produces wisdom; experience must be worked on, organized, reflected upon, and connected to action. Freire locates power inside the classroom — someone is always naming the world for someone else. Skinner irritates but must be kept close: behavior can be shaped whether we like it or not, and the question is what kind of human we produce when training leaves the human behind. Key lesson: she doesn't care about the final product; she cares about the crime scene — the prompts, the friction, the moments where the machine ended and the human had to fight its way out.
points: No theorist is simply wrong — each names something real but incomplete; Piaget's stages became 'a fixed floor plan' while technology kept remodeling the floor underneath.

Vygotsky's insight: education is always relational — you cannot design for adults in crisis as if they were solitary minds downloading content; people need structure plus conversation, mirrors, and another human nearby.

Dewey's corrective: not every experience teaches — experience must be worked on, organized, reflected upon, and connected to action; collecting stories of pain is not the same as asking what can be learned from them.
Freire's warning: someone is always naming the world for someone else and deciding what counts as knowledge and as ignorance — this places power inside every classroom.
On AI writing: don't show the polished output — show the prompts, the friction, the corrections, the moments the machine ended and the human had to fight its way out.
quotes: Montessori... even a liberating pedagogy can become a small church if it stops listening.

There is always language, culture, mediation, imitation, help, and someone else standing nearby. That is useful for my own work because I cannot design anything for adults in crisis as if they were solitary minds downloading content.

Piaget never had to account for a four-year-old swiping a tablet before she can hold a pencil, and yet his stages are still the ruler we use to grid the mind, to chop a moving target into tidy boxes labeled 'appropriate for this age,' as if readiness were a fixed floor plan instead of something technology keeps remodeling underneath us.
Not every experience teaches. Not every activity educates and not every suffering produces wisdom. Experience has to be worked on, organized, reflected upon, and connected to action.

Freire is impossible to ignore because he sees education as a political act, he places power inside the classroom... someone is always naming the world for someone else, and deciding what counts as knowledge and as ignorance.

Skinner, finally, irritates me, which means I have to keep him close... The question is not whether behavior can be trained, but what kind of human being we produce when training leaves the human being behind.

My first lesson: I don't care about the final product; I care about the crime scene... Do not show me what the machine can mimic; show me exactly where the machine ended and the human had to fight its way out.
